rationale: Evidence: iteration 1 (ki 0.4, kp 3.0, kd 0.3, base 1.6, outer sensors at x = ±0.04, sensor_size 0.016) is still the best raced design at 158.144. Iteration 2 showed that cutting speed to 1.2 lowers the score and removes oval finishes, so speed is not the fix (H1 rejected). Iteration 3 widened the outer sensors to x = ±0.06 with speed restored. That scored 54.865, and the oval finish rate fell from 5/20 to 0/20, so H2 (wider outer sensors help) is rejected. Across all runs max_error sits at about 0.061 to 0.063 m, the off-track limit is 0.06 m, and steering oscillation is low (0.11 to 0.22). The failure is steady drift that the controller corrects too slowly on bends, not jitter. Change: revert the sensor geometry to the iteration 1 layout (x = -0.04, -0.02, 0, 0.02, 0.04), which is the only layout with evidence of oval finishes, and raise kp from 3.0 to 3.5 as the stronger steering correction. Everything else stays fixed (ki 0.4, kd 0.3, base_speed 1.6, sensor_size 0.016, weights [-2,-1,0,1,2], last_direction). Expected result: higher progress and fewer off-track exits on s-bend and slalom (progress above 0.2, max_error below 0.06), with the oval finish rate at least 0.25. Hypothesis H3: the bends need more proportional authority than kp 3.0 provides. Measurements to check next: progress and max_error per track, steering_oscillation (if it rises above about 0.35, kd is the next lever), and line_loss_events. If kp 3.5 does not help, the next test is kd 0.5 at the same kp, or a seven-sensor layout that adds x = ±0.04 at a finer pitch.
